topics.title: What is each part for?
topics.summary: Give the reason for every part in a circuit: coupling and bypass capacitors, emitter and base resistors, flyback and protection diodes, gate resistors, and pull-downs.

prerequisiteNotes.schem_passive_blocks: Most "why is this here?" parts are passive blocks doing one small job: a pull-down, a filter, a decoupling capacitor.
prerequisiteNotes.bjt_bias: Emitter resistors, bias dividers, and coupling capacitors exist to set and hold a transistor's operating point.
prerequisiteNotes.diode_practical: Flyback, protection, and reverse-polarity diodes each protect something; knowing how diodes conduct tells you what.

lensNotes.circuit: Nothing on a good schematic is decoration. For each part, ask: what would happen if it were missing, or shorted? The answer is its purpose: remove a flyback diode and the transistor dies at switch-off; remove a coupling capacitor and the bias is upset by the source.
lensNotes.physics: Many parts exist because of physics the ideal models ignore: inductors resist changes in current (flyback diodes), transistors heat up and drift (emitter resistors), and wires have inductance (decoupling capacitors).

goals: Find the job of each part in a circuit by asking what would happen if it were missing or shorted
Explain what the bias divider, emitter resistor, bypass capacitor, and coupling capacitor each do in a common-emitter amplifier, and put numbers on the bias and the gain
Explain why a flyback diode across a coil, a pull-down on a MOSFET gate, and a decoupling capacitor at a chip are needed, from the physics the ideal model leaves out
topics.intuition: Every part on a good schematic is there for a reason; to find it, imagine the part missing or shorted and ask what would go wrong.
topics.why: Many parts exist because real components do things the ideal model ignores. A coil's current cannot change instantly (V = L·di/dt), so when a transistor cuts it off, the coil makes whatever voltage keeps it flowing, often hundreds of volts; a flyback diode gives that current a path instead. A transistor's β and V_BE vary between parts and drift with temperature, so an emitter resistor turns a rise in current into a rise in V_E, which reduces V_BE and pulls the current back. A MOSFET gate is an insulated capacitor that keeps any charge it picks up, so a pull-down holds it off while nothing drives it. Supply wiring has inductance, so a decoupling capacitor supplies fast current spikes from close by.
topics.explanation: "Spotting passive building blocks" taught you to name groups of parts. This topic asks the question engineers ask in a design review: why is this particular part here? The method is always the same: imagine the part removed, then shorted, and ask what changes. In a divider-biased common-emitter amplifier, R1 and R2 set the base voltage. R_E sets the current, I_C ≈ (V_B − 0.7 V)/R_E, nearly independent of β. If I_C rises, V_E rises and V_BE shrinks, so the current is pulled back. That same feedback cuts the signal gain to about R_C/(r_e + R_E), so the capacitor C_E bypasses R_E for signals and the gain rises to about R_C/r_e, with the DC bias untouched. The coupling capacitor passes the signal but blocks DC, so the source cannot drag the base away from its bias. Other parts protect. A flyback diode across a relay coil clamps the voltage at switch-off. A pull-down on a MOSFET gate holds it off while a microcontroller boots. A decoupling capacitor at a chip's pins supplies its current spikes. Each exists because of physics the ideal model leaves out.

workedExample.problem: A common-emitter amplifier runs from 12 V. R1 = 47 kΩ (supply to base) and R2 = 10 kΩ (base to ground) bias the base. R_C = 4.7 kΩ runs from the supply to the collector, and R_E = 1 kΩ from the emitter to ground, with C_E = 100 µF across it. The signal comes from a low-resistance source at 0 V DC, through C1 = 10 µF to the base. Assume V_BE ≈ 0.7 V and β ≈ 100. Say what each part is for, and put numbers on the bias and the gain.
steps: R1 and R2 set the base voltage. Ignoring the small base current, V_B = 12 V × 10 kΩ / (47 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 2.11 V.

R_E sets the current: V_E = 2.11 V − 0.7 V = 1.41 V, so I_E = 1.41 V / 1 kΩ = 1.41 mA ≈ I_C, and β does not appear. (Counting the base current with β = 100 gives about 1.30 mA, 8% lower: β·R_E = 100 kΩ is only about twelve times R1 ∥ R2 = 8.25 kΩ.)
R_C turns that current into a voltage: V_C = 12 V − 1.41 mA × 4.7 kΩ = 5.40 V, well above V_E = 1.41 V and below 12 V, so the collector has room to swing both ways.

Why R_E, by shorting it: the junction would clamp the base near 0.7 V, and R1 would feed it about (12 V − 0.7 V)/47 kΩ − 0.7 V/10 kΩ = 0.17 mA. With β ≈ 100 that asks for 17 mA, far more than R_C allows (12 V / 4.7 kΩ = 2.55 mA), so the transistor saturates. With R_E in place, a rise in I_C raises V_E, lowers V_BE, and pulls I_C back. Even with a divider that avoided saturation, I_C would be β·I_B and would follow each transistor's β and temperature.

Why C_E: r_e = 25 mV / 1.41 mA = 17.8 Ω. With C_E, the emitter is at signal ground and |A_v| ≈ R_C / r_e = 4.7 kΩ / 17.8 Ω = 264. If C_E dries out and opens, |A_v| ≈ 4.7 kΩ / (17.8 Ω + 1 kΩ) = 4.6. C_E carries no DC, so the bias is the same either way.

Why C1, by removing it and wiring the source straight in: the source sits at 0 V DC with a low resistance, so it would pull the base from 2.11 V to nearly 0 V, the transistor would turn off, and V_C would sit at 12 V. With C1 in place, C1 charges once to the 2.11 V difference and then passes only the signal's changes.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 4 "Bipolar Junction Transistors", section "Emitter-bias"
sources.note: Checked that an emitter resistor is negative feedback that holds the emitter current steady against beta and temperature changes, that it also cuts the signal gain, and that a bypass capacitor across it restores the signal gain while the DC bias keeps its stabilization.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 4 "Bipolar Junction Transistors", section "Input and output coupling"
sources.note: Checked that an input coupling capacitor passes the signal while blocking DC, so a low-impedance source cannot pull down the divider's bias voltage on the base.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 3 "Diodes and Rectifiers", section "Inductor commutating circuits"
sources.note: Checked that interrupting a coil's current produces a high voltage spike, and that a reverse-biased diode across the coil gives the current a path and clamps the spike to about one diode drop.

templates.prompt: A logic output switches a relay coil through transistor Q1. D1 sits across the coil, with its cathode on the 12 V supply. What is D1 for?

choices.text: It carries the coil's current when Q1 turns off, so no spike at the collector destroys Q1
choices.feedback: Right: without D1, the coil would force its voltage as high as needed (often hundreds of volts) to keep its current going, and that voltage lands across Q1.

choices.text: It protects Q1 and the coil if the 12 V supply is ever connected backward
choices.feedback: A reverse-polarity diode goes in series with the supply (or across it, backed by a fuse), at the input where the whole circuit's current comes in. D1 sits across the coil and only matters when the coil's own voltage reverses.

choices.text: It makes the relay release faster when Q1 switches off, by draining the coil's stored energy
choices.feedback: It does the opposite: the coil's current circulates through D1 and dies away slowly, so the relay releases a little later. Designs that need a fast release add a Zener or resistor in series with D1.

choices.text: It keeps current flowing through the coil while Q1 is on, so the relay stays pulled in
choices.feedback: While Q1 is on, its collector sits near 0 V, so D1 has 12 V across it the wrong way around: it is reverse biased and carries nothing.

templates.explanation: An inductor resists any change in its current (V = L·di/dt). While Q1 is on, current flows down through the coil; D1 is reverse biased and idle. When Q1 turns off, the coil drives its lower end, the collector, upward to keep that current flowing. As soon as the collector passes about 12.7 V, D1 conducts and the current circulates around the coil–D1 loop until it dies away. Q1 never sees more than about 12.7 V. This is the flyback diode from "LEDs, Zener regulators, and flyback diodes," seen in a real driver.
hints: What does an inductor do when you try to stop its current suddenly?
Is D1 forward or reverse biased while Q1 is on?

followUps.prompt: D1 does nothing while Q1 is on. Why does it start conducting the moment Q1 turns off?

choices.text: The coil keeps its current flowing, driving the collector above 12 V and forward biasing D1
choices.feedback: Right: the collector is D1's anode. Once it rises about 0.7 V above the supply (D1's cathode), D1 conducts and clamps it there.

choices.text: The 12 V supply briefly reverses when Q1 turns off, so D1's cathode goes negative
choices.feedback: The supply stays at 12 V. It is the coil's voltage that reverses, lifting the collector above the supply.

choices.text: Q1's base current has nowhere else to go once Q1 is off, so it flows through D1
choices.feedback: The base circuit is on the other side of Q1 and never connects to D1. The current D1 carries is the coil's current.

choices.text: D1 was conducting all along; it just carries much more of the current after Q1's switch-off
choices.feedback: While Q1 is on, D1's anode (the collector) is near 0 V and its cathode is at 12 V: reverse biased, no current.

followUps.explanation: A coil's current can't stop instantly. When Q1 stops sinking it, the coil makes whatever voltage keeps it flowing, and that drives the collector upward. At about 12.7 V, D1 becomes forward biased and takes over the current, which then decays in the coil's own resistance.

templates.prompt: In this common-emitter amplifier, R1 and R2 bias the base, and R_E sits in the emitter with the large capacitor C_E across it. What is R_E for?

choices.text: It steadies the DC bias: if I_C rises, V_E rises, V_BE shrinks, and I_C falls back
choices.feedback: Right: R_E is DC negative feedback. With the base voltage fixed by R1 and R2, any extra emitter current raises V_E and reduces the transistor's current.

choices.text: It limits the base current so the base-emitter junction isn't damaged
choices.feedback: The base current is only a few microamps, set by the bias. R_E acts on the emitter current, and it does its job by feedback, not by limiting.

choices.text: It sets the voltage gain to about R_C/R_E, so the gain doesn't depend on β
choices.feedback: That would be true if R_E were unbypassed. Here C_E shorts R_E for signals, so the emitter is at signal ground and R_E only acts at DC.

choices.text: It gives the signal a path to ground from the emitter, so the gain stays high
choices.feedback: That is C_E's job. A capacitor passes the signal easily, while R_E carries the DC emitter current.

templates.explanation: R1 and R2 fix V_B at about 2.1 V, so V_E sits one diode drop lower and I_E = V_E/R_E, about 1.4 mA. β hardly matters. If the transistor warms up, or is swapped for one with a higher β, and I_C starts to rise, V_E rises with it. V_B is fixed, so V_BE shrinks and I_C falls back. C_E removes this feedback at signal frequencies so it doesn't cost gain.
hints: The base voltage is fixed by the divider. What happens to V_BE if V_E goes up?

followUps.prompt: Why does a rise in I_C make this circuit pull I_C back down?

choices.text: With V_B held by the divider, a larger I_E·R_E leaves less V_BE, which cuts the current
choices.feedback: Right: a few millivolts less V_BE cuts the current noticeably. The circuit settles where V_E ≈ V_B − 0.7 V.

choices.text: R_E gets hotter with more current, its resistance rises, and that limits the current
choices.feedback: Resistor values barely change with temperature. The effect is electrical: R_E's voltage subtracts from V_BE.

choices.text: The divider current falls when I_C rises, so the base gets less drive and I_C drops
choices.feedback: The divider current is set by R1, R2, and the supply; it hardly changes. It is V_BE, not the divider, that changes.

choices.text: The collector voltage falls as I_C rises, and that lower voltage pushes I_C back down
choices.feedback: In the active region a lower collector voltage barely changes I_C (only the small Early effect). The control is at the base-emitter junction.

followUps.explanation: The transistor's current is set by V_BE = V_B − V_E. V_B is fixed by R1 and R2, and V_E = I_E·R_E. More current means more V_E, less V_BE, and less current: negative feedback that holds I_C near (V_B − 0.7 V)/R_E, as in "Biasing a bipolar transistor."

templates.prompt: In the same amplifier, the signal reaches the base through C1 (10 µF). What is C1 for?

choices.text: It passes the signal but blocks DC, so the source can't upset the bias set by R1 and R2
choices.feedback: Right: C1 lets the signal through while the base stays at its own DC voltage.

choices.text: It filters noise out of the signal before it reaches the transistor
choices.feedback: A 10 µF coupling capacitor is a high-pass with its corner around 10 Hz (with the stage's input resistance of about 1.5 kΩ, taking β ≈ 100): it passes audio and most noise alike. Its job is to block DC, not to filter.

choices.text: It stores charge that gives the transistor extra current on signal peaks
choices.feedback: C1 holds a steady DC voltage (the base voltage) across it; the signal moves only a tiny charge in and out. The transistor's current comes from the 12 V supply.

choices.text: It grounds the base for AC, which keeps the stage stable
choices.feedback: A capacitor from the base to ground would short the input signal away. C1 is in series with the signal path, not across it.

templates.explanation: The base needs a DC voltage of about 2.1 V from R1 and R2, but the signal source usually sits at 0 V DC with a low resistance. Wired straight in, the source would drag the base to 0 V and turn the transistor off. C1 charges to the difference once, then passes the signal's changes through as if it were a wire. C2 does the same at the output, so the next stage or load doesn't see the collector's DC voltage.
hints: A capacitor blocks DC and passes AC. Which DC voltage here must be protected?

followUps.prompt: What would happen if C1 were replaced by a wire and the source sat at 0 V DC?

choices.text: The source would pull the base down to 0 V, so the transistor would switch off and the amplifier would clip or go silent
choices.feedback: Right: the source's low resistance overpowers the 47k and 10k divider. Removing C1 shows its purpose.

choices.text: Nothing much; the signal would just be a little larger
choices.feedback: The problem isn't the signal size but the DC: the source would overrule the bias divider and move the operating point.

choices.text: The transistor would saturate, because more current could flow into the base
choices.feedback: The source at 0 V pulls the base down, not up. Less base voltage means less current: the transistor turns off.

choices.text: The low frequencies would be lost
choices.feedback: Without C1, even DC gets through; if anything, the low end would be extended. The damage is to the bias.

followUps.explanation: Ask what happens when a part is missing to find its purpose. Without C1, the source is connected in parallel with R2. A source with far less resistance than the divider sets the base voltage itself, here 0 V, which is below the 0.7 V the transistor needs.

templates.prompt: This amplifier runs from 12 V with the R1 = 47k / R2 = 10k divider on the base, so V_B ≈ 2.1 V and I_C ≈ (2.1 V − 0.7 V)/R_E = {Ic}. R_C = {Rc}, R_E = {Re} (ignore the load). The bypass capacitor C_E dries out and goes open. What happens to the size of the voltage gain?

whatIf.quantity: the size of the voltage gain

feedback.up: Without C_E, the emitter is no longer at signal ground: it follows the base, so the signal voltage across R_E is subtracted from the input before it reaches the base–emitter junction. That is negative feedback.
feedback.same: C_E carries no DC, so the bias is indeed unchanged. But the gain is about the signal, and for signals C_E was holding the emitter at ground. Without it, the emitter follows the base, and only the difference between them drives the collector current.

templates.explanation: The transistor's own emitter resistance is r_e = 25 mV / I_C = {re}. With C_E in place, the emitter is at signal ground, so the gain is R_C/r_e = {before}. With C_E open, R_E is in the signal path too: gain = R_C/(r_e + R_E) = {after}. R_E stabilizes the bias; C_E stops that stabilizing feedback from also costing gain.
hints: For signals, C_E is nearly a short. What does the emitter do when it is gone?
Gain ≈ R_C divided by the total resistance from emitter to signal ground.
steps: With C_E: the emitter is at signal ground, gain = R_C / r_e = {Rc} / {re} = {before}.

followUps.prompt: C_E is connected straight across R_E. Why doesn't it upset the transistor's DC bias?

choices.text: A capacitor carries no DC current, so the emitter's DC current still has to flow through R_E, and V_E and I_C stay where the bias put them
choices.feedback: Right: at DC, C_E is not there. It only acts on the signal.

choices.text: It does upset it: the bias shifts when C_E is fitted
choices.feedback: Once C_E has charged to V_E, it carries no DC, so the operating point is exactly as without it.

choices.text: C_E is too small to matter at DC
choices.feedback: At 100 µF it is large. Size doesn't matter at DC: an ideal capacitor blocks DC whatever its value.

choices.text: The DC current splits equally between R_E and C_E
choices.feedback: No DC flows through a capacitor. All the emitter's DC current goes through R_E.

followUps.explanation: This is why the pair is used: R_E gives DC negative feedback, which steadies the bias, and C_E removes that feedback for signals, which keeps the gain high. Each part has one job, and the capacitor lets them act at different frequencies.

templates.prompt: A microcontroller pin drives MOSFET Q1 through R1 (100 Ω). R2 (100 kΩ) connects the gate to ground. What is R2 for?

choices.text: It holds the gate at 0 V, so Q1 stays off while the pin is undriven, as at reset
choices.feedback: Right: a floating gate can sit at any voltage. R2 drains its charge so "not driven" means "off."

choices.text: It limits the current from the pin into the gate each time Q1 switches
choices.feedback: That is R1's job: it sits in series with the pin and limits the charging current when the gate switches. R2 goes from the gate to ground, so any current in it is taken away from the gate.

choices.text: It forms a divider with R1 to set the gate voltage Q1 sees when driven
choices.feedback: It does form a divider, but a useless one: 100 kΩ against 100 Ω passes 99.9% of the pin voltage. If a divider were the aim, the values would be comparable.

choices.text: It protects Q1 from the voltage spike at the drain when the load switches off
choices.feedback: Spikes appear at the drain, across the load. They are handled by a flyback diode or snubber there, not by a resistor on the gate.

templates.explanation: A MOSFET's gate is an insulated capacitor: it draws no DC current, so whatever charge reaches it stays. While a microcontroller boots, its pins float, and the gate can drift or pick up charge until Q1 is half on, carrying load current with volts across it, and overheating. R2 is weak enough (100 kΩ) that the pin easily overrides it, but strong enough to pull the gate to 0 V when nothing else drives it: a pull-down, one of the passive blocks from this unit.
hints: What voltage is the gate at when the pin isn't driving it, and R2 is missing?

followUps.prompt: Why can a MOSFET with a floating gate turn itself partly on?

choices.text: The gate is an insulated capacitor, so stray charge stays on it and can sit above threshold
choices.feedback: Right: nothing discharges a floating gate, so its voltage depends on whatever charge happened to arrive.

choices.text: A floating gate is always at 0 V, because no current can flow in to charge it
choices.feedback: No current also means nothing removes charge. A floating gate holds whatever voltage it last had or picked up.

choices.text: The gate needs a steady current to hold it off, and without R2 nothing can supply one
choices.feedback: A MOSFET's gate draws no steady current in either state. It is the gate voltage that decides on or off.

choices.text: Current leaks from the drain through the channel into the gate and slowly charges it up
choices.feedback: The gate is insulated from the channel by an oxide layer. Charge arrives by capacitive coupling (a sudden drain voltage change nudges the gate), not by conduction through the channel.

followUps.explanation: The gate, oxide, and channel form a capacitor, so the gate voltage is charge divided by capacitance. With nothing connected, stray charge sets it, and a few volts is enough to pass the threshold. A pull-down resistor gives that charge a path to ground.

templates.prompt: A logic chip (drawn as its steady load on the supply, plus 10 mA pulses on top when it switches) is fed through about 1 µH of supply wiring. C1, 100 nF, sits right at the chip's supply pin. What is C1 for?

choices.text: It supplies the chip's fast current pulses locally, because the wiring's inductance can't respond that fast
choices.feedback: Right: a decoupling capacitor is a small local store of charge, right where the fast current pulses are drawn.

choices.text: It smooths the ripple from a line-powered rectifier
choices.feedback: A rectifier on 60 Hz line power leaves ripple at 60 or 120 Hz; smoothing it takes a capacitor of hundreds or thousands of µF near the rectifier. 100 nF at the chip does almost nothing at those frequencies; it is aimed at nanosecond pulses.

choices.text: It blocks DC from reaching the chip
choices.feedback: It is connected across the supply, not in series with it. The chip gets its DC straight through the wiring; C1 only helps with fast changes.

choices.text: It keeps the chip running for a moment if the power is cut
choices.feedback: 100 nF holds very little energy: at 10 mA it would drop 1 V in about 10 µs. Hold-up needs far bigger capacitors.

templates.explanation: When a logic chip switches, it draws current pulses lasting a few nanoseconds. Wiring inductance opposes fast changes of current (V = L·di/dt): 1 µH and 10 mA in 10 ns would lose 1 V across the wiring. C1, placed close to the pins, supplies each pulse from its own charge and is topped up slowly through the wiring between pulses, so V_DD stays steady. This is the physics the ideal "wire" ignores. One 10 mA, 10 ns pulse takes only 0.1 nC, which lowers 100 nF by only 1 mV.
hints: Wires have inductance. What does an inductor do to a sudden change of current?

followUps.prompt: Why a 100 nF ceramic rather than a 100 µF electrolytic, which stores far more charge?

choices.text: The electrolytic's internal inductance is several times higher and its ESR far higher, so it can't deliver a nanosecond pulse as cleanly; and each pulse needs only 0.1 nC, which 100 nF supplies with a 1 mV dip
choices.feedback: Right: stored charge isn't the limit here. How fast a capacitor can give up its charge is set by its own series inductance and resistance, and a small ceramic has far less of both.

choices.text: More capacitance would push a bigger current pulse into the chip and could damage it
choices.feedback: A capacitor across the supply doesn't force current into anything: it only holds V_DD. The chip draws the same 10 mA pulse either way; the question is which capacitor can supply it fast enough.

choices.text: A 100 µF capacitor takes too long to charge, so it would never be full
choices.feedback: Through the wiring it charges to V_DD within milliseconds of power-on and then stays there. The limit is how fast it can deliver current during a nanosecond pulse, which its inductance and ESR set.

choices.text: A bigger capacitor across the supply would pull the steady V_DD down
choices.feedback: At DC a capacitor carries no current, so its size has no effect on the steady V_DD. Its only job here is the fast pulses.

followUps.explanation: One 10 mA, 10 ns pulse takes Q = 0.1 nC, and ΔV = Q/C = 0.1 nC / 100 nF = 1 mV: 100 nF already holds plenty. What limits a real capacitor at nanosecond speeds is its equivalent series inductance and resistance (ESL and ESR). A small surface-mount ceramic has about a nanohenry of ESL and tens of milliohms of ESR; a 100 µF aluminum electrolytic, with its wound foil and leads, has several times the inductance and roughly ten times the ESR, so during a fast edge it loses several times more voltage across its own ESL and ESR than the ceramic does. Placement matters as much: pads, vias, and traces add nanohenries of their own, which is why the ceramic sits right at the chip's pins. Boards often use both: an electrolytic for slow, large load changes, and a ceramic at each chip for the fast edges.

templates.prompt: This divider-biased transistor stage runs from {Vcc}. It should read {h0} at the base, {h1} at the emitter, and {h2} at the collector. The meter readings (to ground) are below. Which fault explains them?

fault.netlist:
Bias
VCC vcc 0 {Vcc:spice}
R1 vcc b 47k
R2 b 0 10k
RC vcc c 2.2k
Q1 c b e QN
RE e 0 1k
.model QN NPN

faults.feedback: With R1 open, nothing would feed the base: it would sit at 0 V, the transistor would be off, the emitter would be at 0 V, and the collector would be up at the full supply.
faults.why: The base reads 0 V, so nothing is feeding it: R1 is gone. With no base drive, the transistor is off, so no current flows in R_C and the collector sits at the full {Vcc}.

faults.feedback: With R2 open, R1 alone would feed the base, pushing far more current in: the base and emitter would rise well above normal and the transistor would saturate, with the collector falling close to the emitter.
faults.why: The base is well above its normal voltage, and the collector has dropped to just above the emitter: the transistor is saturated. Only R1 is feeding the base; the leg that holds it down, R2, is missing.

faults.feedback: With R_E shorted, the emitter would read 0 V and the base would be clamped at about 0.7 V; with no R_E feedback, the base drive from R1 would be far more than needed, so the transistor would saturate and the collector would fall to about 0.1 V. Only R_C limits the current.
faults.why: The emitter reads 0 V and the base only about 0.7 V: the base-emitter junction is clamping the divider, because nothing lifts the emitter. With no R_E feedback, the base drive is far more than needed, so the transistor saturates and the collector falls near 0 V; only R_C limits the current.

faults.feedback: With R_C open, no collector current could flow: only the small base current would reach R_E, so the emitter would fall to a fraction of a volt, the base would sit one junction drop above it (under 1 V), and the floating collector would read about the same as the emitter, not the supply.
faults.why: V_B − V_E is still about 0.6 V, so the junction conducts, but V_E is only a fraction of a volt: only base current reaches R_E. With nothing arriving through R_C, the collector floats, held one junction drop below the base by the forward-biased base–collector junction. R_C is open.

faults.text: A solder bridge joins the collector to the emitter
faults.feedback: A collector–emitter bridge would put R_C and R_E in series across the supply: collector and emitter would read the same, the emitter would rise above the base, and the base would sit at the plain divider voltage.
faults.why: The collector and emitter read the same voltage, so something joins them. The emitter is now above the base, which means the transistor is off: the current is going around it, through R_C, the bridge, and R_E.

templates.explanation: Read the three voltages in order. V_E should be about 0.7 V below V_B: if it isn't, the base-emitter junction is off or bypassed. V_E at 0 V with V_B near 0.7 V means R_E is shorted. V_C should be between V_E and the supply: at the supply means no collector current; near V_E with a large V_E means saturated or bridged; near V_E with V_E only a fraction of a volt means the collector is floating (R_C open). Each part's purpose shows up in what goes wrong without it.
hints: Start with V_B − V_E. Is the base-emitter junction still about 0.7 V forward biased?
Then look at the collector: at the supply (no current), in between (normal), or down near the emitter?

templates.prompt: This common-emitter amplifier runs from {Vcc}. R1 = 47 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ bias the base; R_C = 4.7 kΩ and R_E = {Re}. Take V_BE = 0.7 V and ignore the base current (the usual first estimate; with β = 100 the real I_C comes out a few percent lower, up to about 8% here). What DC collector current does R_E set?
templates.explanation: At DC, the capacitors are open, so only the bias parts matter. The divider sets the base: V_B = {Vcc} × 10 kΩ/(47 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = {Vb}. The emitter sits one junction drop lower: V_E = {Vb} − 0.7 V = {Ve}. That voltage is across R_E, so I_E = {Ve}/{Re}, and I_C ≈ I_E = {answer}. This is R_E's job: it turns a fixed base voltage into a fixed current, almost independent of the transistor's β.
hints: Start with the base voltage: which resistor of the divider is it measured across?
The emitter is 0.7 V below the base, and all of that emitter voltage is across R_E.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the whole base voltage across R_E. The emitter sits one base–emitter drop (about 0.7 V) below the base, so R_E only has V_B − 0.7 V across it.
That takes the base voltage as the drop across R1. The base is measured to ground, across R2: V_B = V_CC × R2/(R1 + R2).
That divides by R_C. R_C doesn't set the current; it only turns the current into a collector voltage. The current is fixed by the emitter voltage across R_E.
